messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was thirty-two when his ex-girlfriend, someone he had dated for two years and broken up with eighteen months prior, began appearing at places he frequented. It started with a text message—not threatening, just an observation that she had seen him at a coffee shop he visited every Saturday morning. He had deleted her number months earlier and assumed the contact was accidental. Within a week, she had shown up at the same coffee shop three times. When Marcus changed his routine and went to a different café across town, she found him there too. She began leaving notes on his car. She created fake social media accounts using his name. She called his workplace asking for him, and when his employer mentioned it, Marcus felt the first cold spike of genuine fear—the sense that his movements were being tracked, that no space was truly private anymore.

Over the following months, the stalking intensified. She followed him home from work. She waited outside his apartment building. She sent messages describing what he was wearing, what he had eaten, where he had gone. Marcus filed a police report, obtained a restraining order, changed his phone number. The legal protections felt hollow. He became certain that she was still watching him, that she had simply learned to be more subtle. What terrified him most was not knowing when or where she would appear next—the randomness made every unfamiliar location feel like a trap. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that other people could not be trusted to respect boundaries, that beneath normal social interaction lay the capacity for obsession and violation.

When Marcus met his wife, Elena, two years after the stalking ended, he was cautiously hopeful. The restraining order had held. There had been no contact in nearly a year. But the damage had calcified into something harder to name. He found himself unable to relax in their apartment, even with the doors locked. If Elena suggested they try a new restaurant in an unfamiliar neighborhood, Marcus would feel a surge of panic—he could not assess the danger, could not map exits or anticipate threats. He began declining invitations. He would lie awake beside Elena, listening for sounds that did not exist, his body rigid with the certainty that something was wrong. When she tried to hold him, to be close to him in the way married couples do, he would feel trapped, suffocated by the vulnerability of it. He told himself it was not her fault, that she deserved better, that he was broken in ways he could not fix. He deserved to suffer for not seeing the danger sooner, for not protecting himself well enough. He began spending nights in the spare bedroom, telling Elena he slept better alone.

His work as a tutor—one-on-one sessions in his home office, mostly with high school students preparing for standardized tests—became a minefield. When a student expressed frustration about a difficult problem, raising his voice even slightly, Marcus would feel his nervous system flood with alarm. His chest would tighten. He would struggle to stay present. A few months ago, a student's father came to pick him up and arrived earlier than expected, knocking loudly on the door. Marcus heard the knock and was convinced, for a full minute, that it was her. The panic was so acute that he could not open the door. The father had to call Elena, who came downstairs confused and embarrassed. Marcus had lost two tutoring clients since then—word had gotten out that he was unreliable.

The sound of a motorcycle passing on the street outside could send him into a state of hypervigilance that lasted for hours. He would track the sound, trying to determine if it was circling, if it would return. He had taken to checking the locks on doors and windows obsessively, even though he knew, rationally, that locks would not stop someone determined enough. He knew other people were not all like her, but he could not quite believe it. Everyone seemed to be hiding something. Elena's kindness felt like a performance. His own judgment felt fundamentally broken—if he had missed the signs with his ex, how could he trust himself to see danger or safety accurately now?

It was Elena who finally insisted he seek help. She had given him an ultimatum, not cruelly but clearly: either they go to couples therapy and he gets individual treatment, or she cannot stay. She loves him, she said, but she cannot be a substitute for professional help. Marcus called a therapist last week. He is terrified of what he might learn about himself, but he is more terrified of losing his marriage.
